newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia starts crackdown to clean up government.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia starts crackdown to clean up government.

text.p: Malaysia is starting to crack down on suspected financial abuse among officials, and analysts say this can be a credibility boost for a government sometimes viewed as a protector of the rich and famous.

A lawmaker was charged on Monday with abusing his position by allegedly approving state land for a commercial development, while an aide to a late senior politician was accused in court of accepting a Mercedes Benz to expedite a private project.

Sahar Arpan, the lawmaker in the land case, faces a maximum 14 years imprisonment and fine of 20,000 ringgit. Azman Ghani, the political aide accused of accepting the Mercedes Benz, faces up to to two years in jail if convicted, prosecutors said. Sahar and Azman both pleaded not guilty.

Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim meanwhile sought an explanation from two cabinet ministers on the alleged misappropriation of about 600 million ringgit ($238 million) from a government rubber industry fund.

"I think all these show the government is now more serious in controlling and managing corruption than before," said Abdullah Razak Baginda, executive director of the Malaysian Strategic Resources Centre, a political think-tank.
"At one time, you never saw the big guys fall but now that's changing," added Razak. "I think it's good for the image of the government and political longevity."
Analysts say there is a perception that the high and mighty are sometimes let off quietly.

Stock market participants speculated Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad had planned the crackdown to coincide with his two-month holiday in Europe, during which period Deputy Prime Minister Anwar is in charge.
"He's not around... they can't run to him," said an equities dealer, referring to Mahathir and a popular theory that politicians in trouble often sought his help.
The blitz against high-ranking officials was also read by some analysts as Mahathir's way of testing Anwar, who hopes to succeed him as prime minister whenever he decides he retires.
"A lot could depend on how Anwar handles these matters," said a political observer, who declined to be identified.

For some years now Mahathir has been laying the foundation to combat graft within his political party -- the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) -- through a campaign against what he termed "money politics". UMNO is lynchpin of the ruling National Front party.

But his action has been particularly forceful this year, starting with the chief minister of the economically-vibrant Selangor state, who was caught in Australia's Brisbane airport in January with A$1.2 million in undeclared cash.
Mahathir announced the resignation of Muhammad Muhammad Taib, a vice-president in UMNO, even before the chief minister could clear himself of the court charges in Brisbane.
"I think the government has decided on this line of action for some time now, and it's now bearing fruit," political commentator Rustam Sani said.
In 1995, another chief minister and rising UMNO star was toppled in a corruption scandal.

Rahim Tamby Chik was forced to resign as chief minister of west coast Malacca state and as UMNO youth wing chairman over allegations he had an affair with an underaged girl, as well as of unrelated corruption charges. All the charges were later dropped.
In May of last year, Anwar told parliament that state-run Perwaja Steel suffered accumulated losses of $1.16 billion, partly as a result of mismanagement and irregularities.
Perwaja's former managing director, Eric Chia, handpicked by Mahathir to turn the steelmaker into the centrepiece of Malaysia's industrialisation programme, resigned.
Commentator Rustam, however, said the credibility of the anti-corruption mission ultimately depended on the penalty handed to those found guilty.
"I feel it's already a little late in the day to make any effect on this, if they don't go all the way," Rustam said.
($1=2.52 ringgit)
